nodes.name: Population distribution $F_{XY}$
nodes.statement: Let $F_{XY}$ be a bivariate distribution function with a density $f_{XY}$ and univariate marginals $f_{X}, f_{Y}$.

nodes.name: Biased (weighted) sampling density
nodes.statement: We consider $n$ independent pairs $(X_i,Y_i) \sim F_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y)$ of scalar continuous random variables, sampled from the joint density \begin{equation} f^{(w)}_{X,Y}(x,y)={w}(x,y) f_{XY}(x,y)/\mathbb{E}_{f_{XY}} \{{w}(X,Y)\}, \end{equation} where ${w} : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^+$ is a non-negative weight function such that $0 < \mathbb{E}_{f_{XY}}\{{w}(X,Y)\} < \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Observed pairs are i.i.d. from the density proportional to $w(x,y)f_{XY}(x,y)$, with $w\ge 0$ a weight function of finite positive mean.

nodes.name: Observed marginals $f^{(w)}_X, f^{(w)}_Y$
nodes.statement: The marginals of the observed data are denoted by $f_{X}^{(w)}(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y) dy$ and $f_{Y}^{(w)}(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y) dx$.

nodes.name: Weighted independent density $[f_X f_Y]^{(w)}$
nodes.statement: The weighted independent density is defined as $[f_{X} f_{Y}]^{(w)}(x,y) = {{w}(x,y) f_{X}(x) f_{Y}(y)}/{\mathbb{E}_{f_{X} f_{Y}} \{{w}(X,Y)\}}$, with the corresponding weighted distribution $[F_{X} F_{Y}]^{(w)}$.

nodes.name: Truncation weight function
nodes.statement: An important special case is that of a truncated sample in which \begin{align} {w}(x,y) = \setindicator{\mathcal{A}}(x,y) = \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} 1 & \quad (x,y) \in \mathcal{A} \\ 0 & \quad otherwise, \\ \end{array} \right. \end{align} for some set $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$.

nodes.name: Truncation weight $w=\mathbb{1}_{\mathcal{A}}$
nodes.statement: {w}(x,y) = \setindicator{\mathcal{A}}(x,y) = \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} 1 & \quad (x,y) \in \mathcal{A} \\ 0 & \quad otherwise, \\ \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:truncation_function

nodes.name: Quasi-independence
nodes.statement: (quasi-dependence) We say that the joint distribution $F_{XY}^{(w)}$ is quasi-independent with respect to the weight function ${w}$, if there exist density functions $\tilde{f_{X}}$ and $\tilde{f_{Y}}$, such that \begin{equation} F_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y) \propto \int\displaylimits_{-\infty}^{x}\int\displaylimits_{-\infty}^{y} {w}(s,t) \tilde{f_{X}}(s) \tilde{f_{Y}}(t) dt ds, \quad \forall x,y \in \mathbb{R} \: . \end{equation} Otherwise, we say that $F_{XY}^{(w)}$ is quasi-dependent with respect to the weight function ${w}$.
also_stated_at: However, because $F_{XY}$ is not identifiable on $\{(x,y):{w}(x,y)=0\}$, the goal is restricted to testing quasi-independence defined as $F_{XY}(dx,dy)=\tilde{F}_{X}(dx)\tilde{F}_{Y}(dy)$ for all $(x,y)\in \{(x',y'):{w}(x',y')>0\}$, for some functions $\tilde{F}_{X},\tilde{F}_{Y}$ \citep{tsai1990testing}.
nodes.statement_short: $F^{(w)}_{XY}$ is quasi-independent w.r.t. $w$ if its CDF is proportional to the $w$-tilted product of some densities $\tilde f_X\tilde f_Y$; else quasi-dependent.
nodes.label: def:quasi_independence

nodes.name: Quasi-independence condition
nodes.statement: F_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y) \propto \int\displaylimits_{-\infty}^{x}\int\displaylimits_{-\infty}^{y} {w}(s,t) \tilde{f_{X}}(s) \tilde{f_{Y}}(t) dt ds, \quad \forall x,y \in \mathbb{R} \: .
nodes.label: eq:quasi_independence

nodes.name: Testing quasi-independence
nodes.statement: Based on the sample $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$, we aim at performing the following hypothesis testing for quasi-dependence: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rl} H_0: & F_{XY}^{(w)} \textrm{\; is \; quasi-independent} \\ H_1: & \textrm{otherwise} \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Test $H_0$: $F^{(w)}_{XY}$ is quasi-independent against the alternative, from an i.i.d. biased sample $\mathcal{D}$.

nodes.name: Hypotheses $H_0$ / $H_1$
nodes.statement: \begin{array}{rl} H_0: & F_{XY}^{(w)} \textrm{\; is \; quasi-independent} \\ H_1: & \textrm{otherwise} \end{array}
nodes.label: eq:main_hypothesis_testing

nodes.name: Quasi-dependence implies dependence
nodes.statement: Quasi-dependence implies dependence. When ${w}$ is strictly positive, quasi-dependence is simply dependence of $X$ and $Y$.

nodes.name: Quasi-independence does not imply independence
nodes.statement: Quasi-independence does not imply independence. If ${w}(x,y) = 0$ for some $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, it is possible to have quasi-independence without independence (and then we must have either $\tilde{F_{X}} \neq F_{X}$ or $\tilde{F_{Y}} \neq F_{Y}$). For the important case of $w(x,y)=\mathbbm{1}(x,y)$, \cite{cheng2007nonparametric} discuss the identifiability problem and its implications.
nodes.statement_short: Where $w$ vanishes, quasi-independence can hold without independence, with $\tilde F_X\ne F_X$ or $\tilde F_Y\ne F_Y$.

nodes.name: Unordered samples $\mathcal{D}_x, \mathcal{D}_y$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{D}_x, \mathcal{D}_y$ the unordered samples comprising of $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $\{y_1,\ldots,y_n\}$, respectively.

nodes.name: Partially unordered sample $(x, \mathcal{D}_y)$
nodes.statement: For convenience, we often keep the indices of the original data, but not the coupling between $x,y$, and to this end we use the unordered sample $(x, \mathcal{D}_y)$ - i.e. we keep the original ordering of the $x_i$'s but only the marginal empirical distribution of the $y_i$'s.

nodes.name: Permuted sample $\pi(\mathcal{D})$
nodes.statement: Let $\pi(y)$ be the vector $y$ rearranged according to a permutation $\pi$, i.e. $\pi(y) = (y_{\pi(1)}, .., y_{\pi(n)})$, and let $\pi(\mathcal{D})$ be the permuted sample: $\pi(\mathcal{D}) \equiv \big((x_1, y_{\pi(1)}), .., (x_n, y_{\pi(n)})\big)$.

nodes.name: Weight matrix $\mathcal{W}$
nodes.statement: For a sample $\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$, let $\mathcal{W} \in \mathbb{R}_{n\times n}$ be a weight-matrix defined by $\mathcal{W}(i,j) \equiv {w}(x_i, y_j).$

nodes.name: Weighted permutation distribution $P_{\mathcal{W}}$
nodes.statement: Let $S_n$ be the set of all permutations of $n$ elements, and for $\pi\in S_n$ consider the probability \begin{equation} P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi) \equiv \frac{1}{per(\mathcal{W})} \prod_{i=1}^n \mathcal{W}(i,\pi(i)), \end{equation} where $per(\mathcal{W}) = \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n \mathcal{W}(i, \pi(i))$ is the normalizing constant, given by the permanent of the matrix $\mathcal{W}$.
nodes.statement_short: $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)\propto\prod_i \mathcal{W}(i,\pi(i))$, normalised by the permanent of $\mathcal{W}$.

nodes.name: $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)$
nodes.statement: P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi) \equiv \frac{1}{per(\mathcal{W})} \prod_{i=1}^n \mathcal{W}(i,\pi(i)),
nodes.label: eq:prob_perm

nodes.name: $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ is the null conditional permutation law
nodes.statement: Under $H_0$, the probability $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)$ represents the probability of observing permuted datasets conditional on the marginal sets, that is, $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi(\mathcal{D})) = P_0(\pi \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y)$, where $P_0$ denotes the probability under quasi-independence.
conclusions: the probability $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)$ represents the probability of observing permuted datasets conditional on the marginal sets, that is, $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi(\mathcal{D})) = P_0(\pi \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y)$
nodes.statement_short: Under quasi-independence, the law of the pairing given both marginal samples is $P_{\mathcal{W}}$.
nodes.label: claim:P_W_conditional

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 1
nodes.statement: For a general weighted model, we have \begin{equation} P(\pi(\mathcal{D}) \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi(i)}) }{\sum_{\pi'\in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi'(i)}) }. \end{equation} Under the null, $f_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y)\propto w(x,y)\tilde{f_{X}}(x)\tilde{f_{Y}}(y)$, hence \begin{eqnarray*} P_0(\pi(\mathcal{D}) \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n \tilde{f_{X}}(x_i) \tilde{f_{Y}}(y_{\pi(i)}) \mathcal{W}(i,\pi(i))}{\sum_{\pi' \in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n \tilde{f_{X}}(x_i) \tilde{f_{Y}}(y_{\pi'(i)}) \mathcal{W}(i,\pi'(i))} = P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi). \end{eqnarray*}
also_stated_at: For a general weighted model, we have \begin{equation} P(\pi(\mathcal{D}) \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi(i)}) }{\sum_{\pi'\in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi'(i)}) }. \end{equation} Under the null, $f_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y)\propto w(x,y)\tilde{f_{X}}(x)\tilde{f_{Y}}(y)$, hence \begin{eqnarray*} P_0(\pi(\mathcal{D}) \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n \tilde{f_{X}}(x_i) \tilde{f_{Y}}(y_{\pi(i)}) \mathcal{W}(i,\pi(i))}{\sum_{\pi' \in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n \tilde{f_{X}}(x_i) \tilde{f_{Y}}(y_{\pi'(i)}) \mathcal{W}(i,\pi'(i))} = P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Write the conditional pairing law as a ratio of products of $f^{(w)}$; under the null the $\tilde f$ factors cancel, leaving $P_{\mathcal{W}}$.

nodes.name: Conditional permutation law (general weighted model)
nodes.statement: P(\pi(\mathcal{D}) \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi(i)}) }{\sum_{\pi'\in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi'(i)}) }.
also_stated_at: P(\pi(\mathcal{D}) \mid x, \mathcal{D}_y) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi(i)}) }{\sum_{\pi'\in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi'(i)}) }.
nodes.label: eq:generalperm

nodes.name: Truncation gives the uniform law on valid permutations
nodes.statement: When ${w}(x,y)$ is a truncation function, $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)$ is simply the uniform distribution over the set of valid permutations, i.e. permutations $\pi$ yielding permuted datasets $\pi(\mathcal{D})$ which are consistent with the truncation.
conclusions: $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)$ is simply the uniform distribution over the set of valid permutations

nodes.name: Double randomization lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \sim [F_{XY}^{(w)}]^n$ and conditionally on $\mathcal{D}$ let $\pi$ be a permutation having the conditional probability law given in Equation \eqref{eq:generalperm}. Then $\pi(\mathcal{D}) \sim [F_{XY}^{(w)}]^n$. \begin{proof} Using Equation \eqref{eq:generalperm} and the law of total probability, we have \begin{eqnarray} f_{\pi(\mathcal{D})}\Big((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\Big)& =& \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_i)}{\sum_{\pi'} \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi'(i)}) } \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi(i)}) \nonumber \\ & =& \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_i). \end{eqnarray} \end{proof}
assumptions: conditionally on $\mathcal{D}$ let $\pi$ be a permutation having the conditional probability law given in Equation \eqref{eq:generalperm}
conclusions: $\pi(\mathcal{D}) \sim [F_{XY}^{(w)}]^n$
nodes.statement_short: Permuting an i.i.d. biased sample by its conditional pairing law leaves its distribution unchanged.
nodes.label: lemma:doulbe_randomization

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Using Equation \eqref{eq:generalperm} and the law of total probability, we have \begin{eqnarray} f_{\pi(\mathcal{D})}\Big((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\Big)& =& \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_i)}{\sum_{\pi'} \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi'(i)}) } \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi(i)}) \nonumber \\ & =& \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_i). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Law of total probability over permutations: the sum telescopes to the original product density.

nodes.name: Density of the permuted sample
nodes.statement: f_{\pi(\mathcal{D})}\Big((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\Big)& =& \sum_{\pi \in S_n} \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_i)}{\sum_{\pi'} \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi'(i)}) } \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_{\pi(i)}) \nonumber \\ & =& \prod_{i=1}^n f_{XY}^{(w)}(x_i, y_i).

nodes.name: Derivation of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: Recalling that under the null, Equation \eqref{eq:generalperm} reduces to \eqref{eq:prob_perm} (by Claim \ref{claim:P_W_conditional}), we have
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 3.1 with Claim 1: under the null the conditional law is $P_{\mathcal{W}}$.

nodes.name: Null distribution of $P_{\mathcal{W}}$-permuted data
nodes.statement: Under the null, permuted data points drawn according to Equation \eqref{eq:prob_perm} follow the distribution of $n$ independent copies of $(X,Y) \sim [\tilde {F_{X}} \tilde {F_{Y}}]^{(w)}$.
conclusions: permuted data points drawn according to Equation \eqref{eq:prob_perm} follow the distribution of $n$ independent copies of $(X,Y) \sim [\tilde {F_{X}} \tilde {F_{Y}}]^{(w)}$
nodes.statement_short: Under the null, data permuted by $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ are i.i.d. from the weighted product of the quasi-marginals.
nodes.label: cor:alpha

nodes.name: Test statistic $T$
nodes.statement: Let $T(\mathcal{D})$ be any test statistic.

nodes.name: Permutation P-value
nodes.statement: In practice, a large number of permutations, $B$, is sampled, and the P-value is approximated by \begin{equation} {P}_{value} = \frac{1}{B+1} \sum_{i=0}^{B} \indicator{ T(\pi_i(\mathcal{D})) \geq T(\mathcal{D}) }, \end{equation} where $\pi_0$ is the identity permutation corresponding to $T(\mathcal{D})$.
nodes.statement_short: Empirical P-value: fraction of the $B+1$ permutations (identity included) whose statistic is at least the observed one.

nodes.name: Empirical permutation P-value
nodes.statement: {P}_{value} = \frac{1}{B+1} \sum_{i=0}^{B} \indicator{ T(\pi_i(\mathcal{D})) \geq T(\mathcal{D}) },
nodes.label: eq:empirical_pval

nodes.name: Weighted Permutation Test of Quasi-Independence
nodes.statement: \caption{{\small Weighted Permutation Test of Quasi-Independence}} {\small \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bf Input:} $\mathcal{D}$ - sample, ${w}(x,y)$ - bias function, $T : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}$ - a test statistic \Statex {\bf Parameters:} $B$ - number of permutations \State Generate $B$ permutations $\pi_1,..,\pi_{B} \sim P_{\mathcal{W}}$. \State Compute the test statistic $T_0 \equiv T(\mathcal{D})$. \For{$i=1$ to $B$} \State Compute the test-statistic for the permuted dataset, $T_i = T(\pi_i(\mathcal{D}))$. \EndFor \State {\bf Output:} $P_{value} \equiv \frac{1}{B+1} \sum_{i=0}^{B} \indicator{T_i \geq T_0}$. \end{algorithmic} }
nodes.statement_short: Permutation test with permutations drawn from $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ instead of uniformly; P-value counts permuted statistics $\ge$ the observed one.

nodes.name: Type-1 error control of the weighted permutation test
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{cor:alpha} assures that under the null distribution $P_{value} \sim U[\frac{1}{B+1},...,\frac{B}{B+1},1]$ the type-1 error probability of the weighted permutation test is at most $\alpha$.
conclusions: $P_{value} \sim U[\frac{1}{B+1},...,\frac{B}{B+1},1]$
the type-1 error probability of the weighted permutation test is at most $\alpha$

nodes.name: Current permutation $\pi_t$
nodes.statement: Let $\pi_t = (\pi_t(1),..,\pi_t(n))$ be the permutation at step $t$.

nodes.name: Swap neighbourhood $Neig(\pi_t)$
nodes.statement: Define the neighbours of $\pi_t$ to be all permutations obtained from $\pi_t$ by a single swap, that is, \[ Neig(\pi_t) \equiv\{\pi_t^{i \leftrightarrow j} \equiv \big(\pi_t(1),..\pi_t(j),..,\pi_t(i), .., \pi_t(n)\big),\hspace{0.04in} \forall i < j\}. \]
nodes.genus: permutations obtained from $\pi_t$ by a single swap

nodes.name: MCMC for Biased Sampling of Permutations
nodes.statement: \caption{{\small MCMC for Biased Sampling of Permutations}} {\small \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bf Input:} $\mathcal{D}$ - sample, ${w}(x,y)$ - bias function \Statex {\bf Parameters:} $B$ - number of permutations, $M_0$ - 'burn-in' number of steps, $M$ - number of steps between two permutations. \State Compute $\mathcal{W}(i,j) = {w}(x_i,y_j), \quad \forall i,j=1,..,n$. \State Set $\pi_0$ the identity permutation $\pi_0(i) = i$. \For{$t=0$ to $M_0 + B M - 1$} \State Sample $\pi_t^{i \leftrightarrow j} \sim U [Neig(\pi_t)]$, and $u \sim U[0,1]$. \If {$u \leq \frac{\mathcal{W}(i,\pi_t(j)) \mathcal{W}(j,\pi_t(i))}{\mathcal{W}(i,\pi_t(i))\mathcal{W}(j,\pi_t(j))}$} \State set $\pi_{t+1} \leftarrow \pi_t^{i \leftrightarrow j}$. \Else \State set $\pi_{t+1} \leftarrow \pi_t$. \EndIf \EndFor \State {\bf Output:} The resulting $B$ permutations $\pi_{M_0},\pi_{M_0+M},..,\pi_{M_0+B M}$. \end{algorithmic} }
also_stated_at: We then proceed according to the standard MH algorithm: at each iteration we sample a permutation uniformly from this set $\pi_t^{i \leftrightarrow j} \sim U [Neig(\pi_t)]$, as well as generate a uniform random number $u$ on $[0,1]$. Finally, we accept the new permutation only if \[ u \leq \frac{P(\pi_t^{i \leftrightarrow j})}{P(\pi_t)} = \frac{\mathcal{W}(i,\pi_t(j)) \mathcal{W}(j,\pi_t(i))}{\mathcal{W}(i,\pi_t(i))\mathcal{W}(j,\pi_t(j))}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Metropolis-Hastings on permutations with random transpositions, accepting with the ratio of $\mathcal{W}$ products; thinned output samples $P_{\mathcal{W}}$.

nodes.name: Importance-sampling permutation P-value
nodes.statement: Due to the difficulty of sampling directly from the weighted permutations distribution $P_{\mathcal{W}}$, we propose here another approach: sample permutations $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_B$ according to an importance probability law $P_{IS}$ such that $P_{IS}(\pi)>0$ whenever $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)>0$, and calculate the P-value by \begin{equation} P_{value} \equiv \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{B} \frac{ P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_i)}{ P_{IS}(\pi_i)} \indicator{ T_i \geq T_0 } } {\sum_{i=0}^{B}\frac{P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_i)}{P_{IS}(\pi_i)}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sample permutations from a proposal $P_{IS}$ and weight the indicator $T_i\ge T_0$ by $P_{\mathcal{W}}/P_{IS}$ (self-normalised).

nodes.name: Importance-sampling P-value
nodes.statement: P_{value} \equiv \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{B} \frac{ P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_i)}{ P_{IS}(\pi_i)} \indicator{ T_i \geq T_0 } } {\sum_{i=0}^{B}\frac{P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_i)}{P_{IS}(\pi_i)}}.
nodes.label: eq:IS_pval

nodes.name: Permanent cancels in the IS P-value
nodes.statement: The unknown term $per(\mathcal{W})$ appearing in $P_{\mathcal{W}} $ (see Equation \eqref{eq:prob_perm}) is cancelled in the above equation, thus enabling us to compute the $P_{value}$ even when $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ is known only up to a normalizing constant.

nodes.name: Harrison's conservative importance-sampling test
nodes.statement: \cite{harrison2012conservative} shows that for any test statistic satisfying mild invariance properties, the test that includes the identity permutation in the P-value calculation in Equation \eqref{eq:IS_pval} controls the type-1 error at level $\alpha$ (see his Theorem 1).
assumptions: any test statistic satisfying mild invariance properties
conclusions: the test that includes the identity permutation in the P-value calculation in Equation \eqref{eq:IS_pval} controls the type-1 error at level $\alpha$

nodes.name: Validity of the importance-sampling permutation test
nodes.statement: This result applies directly to our case by considering our approach as testing conditionally on the data $\mathcal{D}$.
conclusions: This result applies directly to our case

nodes.name: Bootstrap-Based Test of Quasi-Independence
nodes.statement: \caption{{\small Bootstrap-Based Test of Quasi-Independence}} {\small \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bf Input:} $\mathcal{D}$ - sample, ${w}(x,y)$ - bias function, $T : \mathbb{R}^{2n} \to \mathbb{R}$ - a test statistic \Statex {\bf Parameters:} $B$ - number of bootstrap samples \State Estimate the marginals $\hat{F}_{X}, \hat{F}_{Y}$. \State Compute the test statistic $T_0 = T(\mathcal{D})$. \For{$i=1$ to $B$} \State Generate a bootstrap sample $\mathcal{D}_i$ by sampling with replacement $n$ i.i.d examples from $[\hat{F}_{X} \hat{F}_{Y}]^{(w)}$. \State Estimate the marginals $\hat{F}_{X,i}, \hat{F}_{Y,i}$ of the bootstrap sample $\mathcal{D}_i$. \State Compute the test statistic $T_i = T(\mathcal{D}_i)$. \EndFor \State {\bf Output:} $P_{value} \equiv \frac{1}{B+1} \sum_{i=0}^{B} \indicator{ T_0 \ge T_i}$. \end{algorithmic} }
nodes.statement_short: Parametric-style bootstrap: resample from the $w$-weighted product of estimated marginals, re-estimate, recompute $T$, compare to $T_0$.

nodes.name: Quasi-marginal variables $\tilde X, \tilde Y$
nodes.statement: Let $\tilde{X}\sim \tilde{F}_X, \tilde{Y}\sim \tilde{F}_Y$, where $\tilde{F}_X,\tilde{F}_Y$ are the cumulative distribution functions of $\tilde{f}_X,\tilde{f}_Y$ in \eqref{eq:quasi_independence}.
nodes.section: 4.2.1 Case 1: Estimating the Marginal Distributions Under Quasi-independence

nodes.name: Observed $X$-density under quasi-independence
nodes.statement: Under quasi-independence, by the law of total probability, the density of $X$ can be written as ${f}_{X}(x)=\mathbb{E}\{w(x,\tilde{Y})\}\tilde{f}(x)/\mathbb{E}\{w(\tilde{X},\tilde{Y})\}$.
nodes.section: 4.2.1 Case 1: Estimating the Marginal Distributions Under Quasi-independence
conclusions: the density of $X$ can be written as ${f}_{X}(x)=\mathbb{E}\{w(x,\tilde{Y})\}\tilde{f}(x)/\mathbb{E}\{w(\tilde{X},\tilde{Y})\}$

nodes.name: Inverse-weighting update for $\tilde F_X$
nodes.statement: Thus, an estimate of $\tilde{F}_Y$ yields an estimate for $\mathbb{E}\{w(x,\tilde{Y})\}$, which can be used to build an inverse weighting estimate for $\tilde{F}_X$: \begin{equation} \widehat{\tilde{F}}_X(x)= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{x_{i}\le x} \hat{\mathbb{E}}\{w(x_i,\tilde{Y})\}^{-1}} {\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{\mathbb{E}}\{w(x_i,\tilde{Y})\}^{-1}}. \end{equation}

nodes.statement_short: Estimate $\tilde F_X$ by weighting each $x_i$ by the inverse of the estimated $\mathbb{E} w(x_i,\tilde Y)$.

nodes.name: Inverse-weighting update
nodes.statement: \widehat{\tilde{F}}_X(x)= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{x_{i}\le x} \hat{\mathbb{E}}\{w(x_i,\tilde{Y})\}^{-1}} {\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{\mathbb{E}}\{w(x_i,\tilde{Y})\}^{-1}}.

nodes.name: Reduction to the product-limit estimator under truncation
nodes.statement: For the important case ${w}(x,y) = \indicator{x<y}$, the algorithm reduces to the standard product-limit (PL) estimator for left and right truncated data, implemented, for example, in the DTDA package of R \citep{moreira2010dtda}.

nodes.name: Estimation of Marginal Distributions Under Quasi-independence
nodes.statement: \caption{{\small Estimation of Marginal Distributions Under Quasi-independence}} {\small \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bf Input:} $\mathcal{D}$ - sample, ${w}(x,y)$ - bias function, $d(F_1,F_2)$ - distance function. \Statex {\bf Parameters:} $\epsilon$ - convergence criterion. \State Generate initial estimates $\tilde F^{new}_X,\tilde F^{new}_Y$ and set $\tilde F^{old}_X=\tilde F^{old}_Y\equiv 0$. \While{$d(\tilde F^{old}_X,\tilde F^{new}_X)+d(\tilde F^{old}_Y,\tilde F^{new}_Y)>\epsilon$} \State Set $\tilde F^{old}_X=\tilde F^{new}_X$ and $\tilde F^{old}_Y=\tilde F^{new}_Y$. \State Calculate $\mathbb{E}_{\tilde F^{new}_{Y}}\{w(x,{Y})\}$, and update $\tilde F^{new}_X$ using \eqref{eq:estim_update}. \State Calculate $\mathbb{E}_{\tilde F^{new}_{X}}\{w({X},y)\}$, and update $\tilde F^{new}_Y$ using the equivalent for $\tilde{F}_Y$ of \eqref{eq:estim_update}. \EndWhile \State {\bf Output:} $\tilde F^{new}_X$ and $\tilde F^{new}_Y$. \end{algorithmic} }

nodes.statement_short: Alternate inverse-weighting updates of $\tilde F_X$ and $\tilde F_Y$, each using the other's current estimate, until the estimates stabilise.

nodes.name: Null-consistent marginals give low power
nodes.statement: While Algorithm \ref{alg:est_marg} provides a general procedure to estimate a distribution under independence, for testing purposes it may result in low power. Consider the truncation model ${w}(x,y) = \indicator{x<y}$. The PL estimators are consistent under the null hypothesis, but using them in our test leads to low power, even in seemingly very extreme situations of a strong dependence. For a test to perform reasonably well for moderate sample sizes, $F_{X}$ and $F_{Y}$ should be estimated well not only under the null, but also under the alternative hypothesis (see Section \ref{sec:simulations} and Supp. Materials, Section B). The next example demonstrates this claim.
nodes.section: 4.2.1 Case 1: Estimating the Marginal Distributions Under Quasi-independence
nodes.statement_short: Marginal estimates consistent only under the null (e.g. PL under truncation) make the bootstrap test weak; they should be consistent under the alternative too.

nodes.name: Difficulties in Detecting Quasi-Independence
nodes.statement: \noindent \textbf{Example: Difficulties in Detecting Quasi-Independence} Consider the case where data is generated from a uniform bivariate distribution over $\{0 < x, y < 1: \hspace{0.03in} |x − y| < 0.3\}$, and let ${w}(x,y)=\indicator{x<y}$ be the standard truncation model. We drew $n=500$ samples from this model and estimated the univariate marginals CDFs using the PL estimators. The left panel of Figure \ref{example} shows the sampled data points. The green and red curves in the right panel are the resulting PL estimates of $\tilde{F}_X$ and $\tilde{F}_Y$, respectively. Because the unbiased variables $\tilde{X}$ and $\tilde{Y}$ are exchangeable, they share the same underlying marginal distribution, depicted by the blue line. The product-limit estimates differ considerably from the true marginal distribution. When such CDFs generate the truncated data, the probability of a selection $(\tilde X < \tilde Y)$ is small, and when it happens, the values of $\tilde X$ and $\tilde Y$ tend to be close, yielding a scatter plot somewhat similar to the observed data. Indeed, the middle panel of Figure \ref{example} shows pairs obtained by generating independent variables from the estimated product-limit curves $\hat{F}_{X}$, $\hat{F}_{Y}$ and retaining only observations satisfying $\tilde X< \tilde Y$. This example shows that independent variables under selection bias can produce data similar to that obtained by strongly dependent variables. Applying the bootstrap test using estimates of the marginal that are consistent only under the null independence assumption may result in a test with low power.

nodes.name: Non-identifiability under the alternative
nodes.statement: A possible solution is to find estimators for the marginal CDFs that are consistent also under the alternative hypothesis of quasi-dependence. However, as the model is not identifiable under the alternative \citep{cheng2007nonparametric}, such estimators can be calculated only under additional assumptions, either on ${w}(x,y)$, or on the underlying joint distribution (or both).

nodes.name: NPMLE under weighted sampling
nodes.statement: The problem of estimating non-parametrically a general multivariate distribution $F$ using weighted data is well known (e.g., \cite{vardi1985empirical}) and for $w>0$ the non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) is given by: \begin{equation} \hat{F}_{XY}^n(t, s) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \indicator{X_i\leq t, Y_i\leq s}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}}. \end{equation}
conclusions: the non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) is given by
nodes.statement_short: For positive $w$, the NPMLE of $F_{XY}$ from weighted data is the empirical CDF reweighted by $1/w$.

nodes.name: NPMLE $\hat F^n_{XY}$
nodes.statement: \hat{F}_{XY}^n(t, s) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \indicator{X_i\leq t, Y_i\leq s}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}}.
nodes.label: eq:non_parametric_MLE

nodes.name: Inverse-weighted marginal estimator
nodes.statement: Estimators for $F_{X}$ and $F_{Y}$ can be then obtained by marginalization of Equation \eqref{eq:non_parametric_MLE}, \begin{equation} \hat{F}_{X}^n(t) =\hat{F}_{XY}^n(x, \infty) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \indicator{X_{i}\leq t}w(X_i,Y_i)^{-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Marginal estimator $\hat F^n_X$
nodes.statement: \hat{F}_{X}^n(t) =\hat{F}_{XY}^n(x, \infty) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \indicator{X_{i}\leq t}w(X_i,Y_i)^{-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}}.
nodes.label: eq:marginal_estimation_under_positive_weight_function

nodes.name: Consistency of inverse-weighted marginals for $w>0$
nodes.statement: By the law of large numbers, $n^{-1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \indicator{X_{i}\leq t}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}}\to F_X(t)/\mathbb{E}_{f_{XY}} \{{w}(X,Y)\}$ a.s. and $n^{-1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w(X_i, Y_i)^{-1}} \to 1/\mathbb{E}_{f_{XY}} \{{w}(X,Y)\}$ a.s. so by the continuous mapping theorem $\hat{F}_{X}^n(t) \to F_{X}(t)$ a.s. By similar arguments, $\hat{F}_{Y}^n(s) \to F_{Y}(s)$ a.s.
conclusions: $\hat{F}_{X}^n(t) \to F_{X}(t)$ a.s.
$\hat{F}_{Y}^n(s) \to F_{Y}(s)$ a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Law of large numbers plus continuous mapping: the inverse-weighted marginal estimators are strongly consistent when $w>0$.

nodes.name: Consistent marginals under exchangeability and left truncation
nodes.statement: Let $F_{XY}(x,y)$ be an exchangeable joint distribution having a density $f_{XY}(x,y) \equiv f_{XY}(y,x)$ and let $\mathcal{D} \sim [F_{XY}^{(w)}]^n$ be a sample with the truncation weight function ${w}(x,y) = \indicator{x<y}$. Let $\hat{F}^{(w),n}_X, \hat{F}^{(w),n}_Y$ be the empirical CDFs of $F_{X}^{(w)}, F_{Y}^{(w)}$, respectively. Define: \begin{equation} \hat{F}_{X}^n(x) = \hat{F}_{Y}^n(x) = \frac{\hat{F}^{(w),n}_X(x)+\hat{F}^{(w),n}_Y(x)}{2}=\frac{1}{2n}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{X_i\le x} + \sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{Y_i\le x} \Big]. \end{equation} Then $\hat{F}_{X}^n, \hat{F}_{Y}^n \to F_{X}=F_{Y}$ a.s.

conclusions: Then $\hat{F}_{X}^n, \hat{F}_{Y}^n \to F_{X}=F_{Y}$ a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Under exchangeability and truncation $x<y$, the pooled empirical CDF of all $X_i$ and $Y_i$ is strongly consistent for the common marginal.

nodes.name: Pooled estimator
nodes.statement: \hat{F}_{X}^n(x) = \hat{F}_{Y}^n(x) = \frac{\hat{F}^{(w),n}_X(x)+\hat{F}^{(w),n}_Y(x)}{2}=\frac{1}{2n}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{X_i\le x} + \sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{Y_i\le x} \Big].
nodes.label: eq:exchange_estimator

nodes.name: Data quadrants $Q_i^{jk}$
nodes.statement: Specifically, each data point $(x_i,y_i) \in \mathcal{D}$ defines a partition of $\mathbb{R}^2$ into four quadrants: \begin{equation} Q_{i}^{jk} \equiv \Big\{(x',y') \in \mathbb{R}^2 \: : \: \indicator{x'>x_i} = j, \indicator{y'>y_i} = k \Big\} \quad j,k \in \{0,1\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Quadrants $Q_i^{jk}$
nodes.statement: Q_{i}^{jk} \equiv \Big\{(x',y') \in \mathbb{R}^2 \: : \: \indicator{x'>x_i} = j, \indicator{y'>y_i} = k \Big\} \quad j,k \in \{0,1\}.
nodes.label: eq:data_quartiles_def

nodes.name: Observed and expected quadrant counts
nodes.statement: For a quadrant $Q_i^{jk}$, we denote the observed number of points by $o_{i}^{jk} \equiv o_{Q_i^{jk}}$ and the expected number of points under the null by $e_{i}^{jk} \equiv e_{Q_i^{jk}}$.

nodes.name: Adjusted Hoeffding statistic
nodes.statement: We then compute, for each quadrant, the scaled squared difference between the observed and expected number of points under $H_0$. Finally, we sum over all the sample points to get our test statistic: \begin{equation} T = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j,k \in \{0,1\}} \frac{(o_{i}^{jk}-e_{i}^{jk})^2}{e_{i}^{jk}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sum over sample points and their four quadrants of Pearson chi-square terms $(o-e)^2/e$.

nodes.name: Wrong expectations keep validity but cost power
nodes.statement: Estimating the expected values $e_{i}^{jk}$ requires the estimation of the null distribution, which may become highly non-trivial in the biased sampling setting. First, $F_{X}$ and $F_{Y}$ may be un-identifiable, and therefore using plug-in estimators of $F_{X}, F_{Y}$ may give a poor approximation of the distribution of the test statistic under the null. Second, evaluation of expectations or probabilities under the null may require computationally costly integration of the null distribution, $[f_{X} f_{Y}]^{(w)}$, as opposed to a simple multiplication of the empirical marginals in the standard setting. If the expectations $e_{i}^{jk}$ are not estimated correctly, the WP test is still valid according to Corollary \ref{cor:alpha} and the bootstrap approach can be also applied, but power can be severely reduced, as is shown in the Supp. Materials, Section \ref{sec:fast_bootstrap}.
nodes.statement_short: Null expectations are hard under biased sampling; mis-estimated ones leave the WP test valid (Corollary 1) but can severely reduce power.

nodes.name: Pairing probabilities $P_{ij}$
nodes.statement: Let $P_{ij} \equiv P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi(i)=j) = \sum_{\pi \in S_n} P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi) \indicator{ \pi(i)=j }$, and define the Bernoulli random variables $\xi^\pi_{ij} \equiv \indicator{\pi(i) = j }$, so $P_{ij} = \mathbb{E}(\xi^\pi_{ij})$.

nodes.name: Permuted counts $o_{\mathcal{A}}(\pi)$ and expected count $e_{\mathcal{A}}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be an arbitrary set. Given a sample $\mathcal{D}$, for any permutation $\pi$ of the data, denote the number of points in $\mathcal{A}$ under $\pi$ (i.e., after permuting the data set $\mathcal{D}$) by $o_{\mathcal{A}}(\pi)= \sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{ (x_i,y_{\pi(i)}) \in {\mathcal{A}} }$, and let $e_{\mathcal{A}} \equiv \mathbb{E}_{P_{\mathcal{W}}} \{o_{\mathcal{A}}(\pi)\}$ be the expected number of data points in $\mathcal{A}$, under the permutations distribution $P_{\mathcal{W}}$.

nodes.name: Expected counts from pairing probabilities
nodes.statement: For any $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, the expected number of points $e_{\mathcal{A}}$ under the permutations distribution $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ is given by: \begin{equation} e_{\mathcal{A}} = \sum_{i,j=1}^n \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{P_{\mathcal{W}}}(\xi^\pi_{ij}) = \sum_{i,j=1}^n \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{ij} . \end{equation} \begin{proof} By definition, we have: \begin{equation} e_{\mathcal{A}} = \mathbb{E}_{P_{\mathcal{W}}} \big[\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{ (x_i,y_{\pi(i)}) \in \mathcal{A} }\big] = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{\mathcal{W}}\big( \pi(i)=j \big) = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{ij}. \end{equation} \end{proof}
conclusions: the expected number of points $e_{\mathcal{A}}$ under the permutations distribution $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ is given by:
nodes.statement_short: $e_{\mathcal{A}}=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb{1}\{(x_i,y_j)\in\mathcal{A}\}P_{ij}$.
nodes.label: claim:expected_permutations

nodes.name: $e_{\mathcal{A}}$ via $P_{ij}$
nodes.statement: e_{\mathcal{A}} = \sum_{i,j=1}^n \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{P_{\mathcal{W}}}(\xi^\pi_{ij}) = \sum_{i,j=1}^n \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{ij} .
nodes.label: eq:expected_region

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: By definition, we have: \begin{equation} e_{\mathcal{A}} = \mathbb{E}_{P_{\mathcal{W}}} \big[\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{ (x_i,y_{\pi(i)}) \in \mathcal{A} }\big] = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{\mathcal{W}}\big( \pi(i)=j \big) = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{ij}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Linearity of expectation over the indicators $\pi(i)=j$.

nodes.name: Expansion of $e_{\mathcal{A}}$
nodes.statement: e_{\mathcal{A}} = \mathbb{E}_{P_{\mathcal{W}}} \big[\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{ (x_i,y_{\pi(i)}) \in \mathcal{A} }\big] = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{\mathcal{W}}\big( \pi(i)=j \big) = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} P_{ij}.

nodes.name: MCMC estimator $\hat P_{ij}$
nodes.statement: The probabilities $P_{ij}$ can be easily estimated using the MCMC scheme described in Algorithm \ref{alg:mcmc_permutations}: let $\pi_0$ be the identity permutation and $\pi_1, .., \pi_{B}$ be the sampled permutations, and define the following estimator: \begin{equation} \hat{P}_{ij} \equiv \frac{1}{B+1} \sum_{b=0}^B \indicator{\pi_b(i)=j}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: $\hat P_{ij}$
nodes.statement: \hat{P}_{ij} \equiv \frac{1}{B+1} \sum_{b=0}^B \indicator{\pi_b(i)=j}.
nodes.label: eq:P_ij_estimator

nodes.name: Importance-sampling estimator $\hat P^{(IS)}_{ij}$
nodes.statement: When we sample permutations using an importance distribution $P_{IS}$ (see Section \ref{sec:importance_sampling}), the above estimator for ${P}_{ij}$ is replaced by: \begin{equation} \hat{P}_{ij}^{(IS)} \equiv \frac{\sum_{b=0}^B \indicator{\pi_b(i)=j} \frac{P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_b)}{P_{IS}(\pi_b)} }{\sum_{b=0}^B \frac{P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_b)}{P_{IS}(\pi_b)}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: $\hat P^{(IS)}_{ij}$
nodes.statement: \hat{P}_{ij}^{(IS)} \equiv \frac{\sum_{b=0}^B \indicator{\pi_b(i)=j} \frac{P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_b)}{P_{IS}(\pi_b)} }{\sum_{b=0}^B \frac{P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_b)}{P_{IS}(\pi_b)}}.
nodes.label: eq:P_ij_estimator_IS

nodes.name: Estimated expected count $\hat e_{\mathcal{A}}$
nodes.statement: Plugging Equation \eqref{eq:P_ij_estimator} (or Equation \eqref{eq:P_ij_estimator_IS}) into Equation \eqref{eq:expected_region} gives an estimator of $e_{\mathcal{A}}$, \begin{equation} {\hat{e}}_{\mathcal{A}} = \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \indicator{(x_i,y_j) \in \mathcal{A}} \hat{P}_{ij}, \end{equation} which can be used in the Chi-squared statistic.

nodes.name: Left-truncation right-censoring model
nodes.statement: Consider the standard left-truncation right-censoring model where $(X_i,Y_i, C_i)$ are $n$ independent triplets, the joint density of $(X_i,Y_i)$ is proportional to $f_{XY}(x,y)\setindicator{\{x<y\}}$ for some density $f_{XY}$, and $(X_i,Y_i)$ are independent of the censoring variables $C_i$.

nodes.name: Censoring indicators $\Delta_i$
nodes.statement: We observe triplets $(X_i,\min(Y_i,X_i+C_i),\Delta_i$), where $\Delta_i=\setindicator{\{Y_i< X_i+C_i\}}$ are the censoring indicators with $\Delta_i=0$ and $1$ for censored and uncensored observations, respectively.

nodes.name: Weighted test for left-truncated right-censored data
nodes.statement: We suggest testing independence based on the uncensored observations, where censored observations are used only for estimation of the weight function. Specifically, the conditional density of an uncensored observation is simply \begin{equation} \frac{S(y-x)f_{XY}(x,y)\setindicator{\{x<y\}}}{\mathbb{E}_{f_{XY}}[S( Y- X)\setindicator{\{ X< Y\}}]}, \end{equation} where $S(t)=P(C>t)$ is the survival function of $C$. Thus, the density of uncensored observations has exactly the form of Equation \eqref{eq:weighted_density}, with $w(x,y)=\setindicator{\{x<y\}} S(y-x)$, a function involving a continuous and a truncated part. The methods developed in previous sections are flexible enough to accommodate such functions. The survival function $S$ can be estimated by the standard Kaplan-Meier estimator applied to the data $\{(\min(C_i,Y_i-X_i),1-\Delta_i), \: i=1,\ldots,n \}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Since $X$ and $Y$ are continuous exchangeable random variables, $P(X< Y)=1/2$ and therefore $$ f_{XY}^{(w)}(x,y)=2\indicator{x < y} f_{XY}(x,y). $$ Calculating the weighted marginal, we have $$ f_{X}^{(w)}(t)=2\int_t^\infty f_{XY}(t,y)dy=2\int_t^\infty f_{XY}(y,t)dy, $$ due to exchangeability. Similarly $$ f_{Y}^{(w)}(t)=2\int_{-\infty}^t f_{XY}(x,t)dx . $$ Thus (due to the continuity assumption), $$ \frac{f_{X}^{(w)}(t)+f_{Y}^{(w)}(t)}{2}=\int_t^\infty f_{XY}(y,t)dy+\int_{-\infty}^t f_{XY}(x,t)dx = f_{Y}(t). $$ The result follows by applying the Glivenko–Cantelli Theorem on $\hat{F}^{(w),n}_X$ and $\hat{F}^{(w),n}_Y$ .
nodes.statement_short: With $P(X<Y)=1/2$, write both weighted marginals as integrals of $f_{XY}$; by exchangeability their average is $f_Y$; conclude by Glivenko-Cantelli.

nodes.name: Uniform grid importance sampling
nodes.statement: The 'uniform grid' method interpolates between the uniform method, that produce permutations with $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)$ too low, and the monotonic method that produce permutations with $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi)$ that may be too high. nodes.statement: \caption{{\small SIS Permutation Test of Quasi-Independence }} {\small \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bf Input:} $\mathcal{D}$ - sample, ${w}(x,y)$ - bias function. \Statex {\bf Parameters:} $B$ - number of permutations. \State Compute $\mathcal{W}(i,j) = {w}(x_i,y_j), \quad \forall i,j=1,..,n$. \State Set $\pi_0$ the identity permutation $\pi_0(i) = i$. \For{$b=1$ to $B$} \State Initialize the importance sampling and weighted (unnormalized) probabilities \hspace{1cm} $\quad \quad P_{IS}(\pi_b)=P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_b)=1$. \State Compute $V_i = Var\Big(\log(\mathcal{W}(i,1)),..,\log(\mathcal{W}(i,n))\Big), \quad \forall i=1,..,n$. \State Order the variables by decreasing order of $V_i$: $V_{\sigma(1)} \geq ... \geq V_{\sigma(n)}$. \For {$i=1$ to $n$} \State Sample $\pi_{b}(\sigma(i))$ with probabilities: \\ \hspace{3cm} $Pr(\pi_{b}(\sigma(i))=j) \propto \mathcal{W}(\sigma(i),j) \prod_{k=1}^{i-1} \indicator{\pi_b(\sigma(k)) \neq j}$. \State Update the probability $P_{IS}(\pi_{b}) = P_{IS}(\pi_{b}) \times \frac{\mathcal{W}(\sigma(i),\pi_{b}(i))}{\sum_{j=1}^n \mathcal{W}(\sigma(i),j) \prod_{k=1}^{i-1} \indicator{\pi_b(\sigma(k)) \neq j}}$ . \State Update the (unnormalized) probability $P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_{b}) = P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_{b}) \times \mathcal{W}(\sigma(i),\pi_{b}(i))$ . \EndFor \EndFor \State {\bf Output:} $P_{value}$ computed from the $P_{IS}(\pi_b),P_{\mathcal{W}}(\pi_b)$'s according to Equation \eqref{eq:IS_pval}. \end{algorithmic} }

nodes.statement: \caption{{\small Estimation of Marginals Under Quasi-independence}} {\small \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bf Input:} $(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik})$ ($i=1,\ldots,n$) - sample, $w$ - bias function, $d(F_1,F_2)$ - distance function. \Statex {\bf Parameters:} $\epsilon$ - convergence criterion. \State Generate initial estimates using Equation (\ref{naive}), and set $ F^{new}_j=\hat{F}^n_j$, $ F^{old}_j\equiv 0$. \While{$\max_j d( F_j^{old}, F_j^{new})<\epsilon$} \State Set $ F^{old}_j=F^{new}_j$ $(j=1,\ldots,k)$. \For{$j=1,\ldots,k$} \State Calculate $e^{new}_{ij}={\tilde{E}}(w; j,x_{ij})$ with respect to $\prod_{\ell=1}^k F_\ell^{new}$, for all $x_{ij}$ $(i=1,\ldots,n)$. \State Set $$ F^{new}_j(x)= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \indicator{x_{ij}\le x} [e^{new}_{ij}]^{-1}} {\sum_{i=1}^n [e^{new}_{ij}]^{-1}}. $$ \EndFor \EndWhile \State {\bf Output:} $F^{new}_1,\ldots,F^{new}_k$. \end{algorithmic} }

nodes.name: Linear weight gives $O(n)$ update
nodes.statement: For the important case of a linear weight function, the calculation of ${\tilde{E}}(w; j,x_{ij})$ is rather simple. Let $w({\bf x})={\bf a}^{t}{\bf x}+b$, where the vector $\bf a$ and the constant $b$ are known ($\bf a\equiv 1$ and $b=0$ is the sum-bias case $w(\textbf{x})=x_1+\cdots+x_k$). Thus, the computational complexity of each step $5$ reduces to $O(n)$.
